title: Peck Kelley's self-taught piano style
summary: Teagarden describes Kelley's self-teaching, practice, classical influences and how overwhelming his playing was.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Can we back up for a minute and go back to your early period? Yeah. Because there's some particular people I'd like to ask you about some particular things. What kind of training did Peg Kelly have that he should develop this wonderful style?

Well, he's self-taught, but he used to listen to, uh, everybody that came through Houston. Especially, there used to be quite a few colored boys that come through Houston, you know, from New Orleans. Yeah. And there was quite, quite a lot of, uh, entertainment in that city at that time. And, uh, I guess he picked up a little bit here and there from everybody and they put it all with his own. And, uh, it was fantastic when I first heard him and, uh, I guess he still is now. I saw him just a few weeks ago. I didn't hear him play because, uh, his piano at home is, uh, not in very good condition. But, uh, they tell me that he keeps up his practice every day. On, sometimes on a silent keyboard and, and what time he goes out. But he doesn't work professionally anymore.

You know, he seems to me to have been so wonderful and to develop a lot of things that, you know, from what I've heard from Len Harrell and guys who listen to him. Yeah. Yeah. Like the guy who worked with Jimmy Joy, Len Harrell, I'm talking about. Yeah. He must have heard a lot of classical music too, huh?

Yeah. He went, he made a, he made a real study of piano. He used to practice about eight hours a day. And, uh, he taught himself to read and then he, uh, went for Chopin mostly. And, uh, of course, uh, Debussy and, uh, and Ravel. And he made, uh, put all this with his ideas. And, uh, of course he knows Boogie Woogie and, uh, and the Earl Hines style of piano. He was playing long before, way before Earl Hines. And I guess it, uh, never been heard by anybody. He was sort of, uh, Art Tatum maybe. Uh, Art Tatum and Earl Hines together. And that's Walter, near as I can describe it. And you put them with, their ideas with, uh, Debussy's, uh, themes and things. Well, it's, it's tremendous. And he used to leave me and just fell down. I mean, I could listen to him play for a while and it would, uh, I couldn't hardly get up out of a chair. It was, uh, like a real, uh, a real wonderful moving picture. It would, uh, for, you know, that makes you laugh and you cry. And there's so many emotions that goes with your listening to him play that it leaves you just worn out.

Well, to me, and when I listen to your style, I see that you have developed such a clean technique and developed the trombone so much further than the people that were before you. I believe myself. Yeah.
